notes.heading: Add signed displacements and identify the boundary conditions
paragraphs: For linear superposition, instantaneous displacements add algebraically. Opposite signs may cancel at one place and time without making either travelling wave disappear. A stationary pattern has persistent nodes because interference repeatedly cancels there. Allowed wavelengths depend on the boundary conditions: a string fixed at both ends differs from an ideal air column closed at one end. State the system before using a harmonic formula. Frequency, phase and displacement are distinct quantities, so do not infer a wave's complete behaviour from one instantaneous measurement.

questions.prompt: At one point and instant, two small transverse waves produce displacements +3 mm and -5 mm under linear superposition. Find the resultant and explain whether either wave has been permanently destroyed.
questions.answer: Resultant displacement -2 mm. The waves continue propagating; the sum describes this point and instant.
solution: Distinguish local instantaneous interference from permanent removal of a wave.

questions.prompt: An ideal air column of length 0.85 m is closed at one end and open at the other, with sound speed 340 m/s. Ignoring end correction, find its fundamental and next allowed resonance frequency.
questions.answer: Fundamental 100 Hz; next allowed resonance 300 Hz.
solution: The fundamental has wavelength 4L=3.4 m, so f=v/λ=100 Hz.
For these boundary conditions only odd harmonics occur in the ideal model.
markingPoints: Find next resonance 300 Hz and explain odd harmonics.

questions.prompt: Adjacent nodes of an ideal stationary wave are 0.40 m apart. Find the constituent wavelength and the distance from a node to its nearest antinode.
questions.answer: Wavelength 0.80 m; nearest node-antinode separation 0.20 m.
solution: A nearest antinode is halfway between adjacent nodes, at λ/4.
